chunks: "Both are coils that turn electrical energy into mechanical motion using magnetic force, and both are inductive loads, so both kick back when you switch them off and need a flyback diode.
The difference is the kind of motion and how they behave electrically. A motor makes continuous rotation.
The torque comes from current in the windings sitting in a magnetic field, so torque is proportional to current, and as it spins it generates a back-EMF that limits the current.
You get a smooth torque-speed curve and can run it forever. A solenoid is a coil with a movable iron plunger, and it gives a short linear stroke.
Energise it and the plunger gets pulled in to close the magnetic gap.
The force is roughly proportional to current squared and it's strongest when the gap is smallest, falling off quickly as the gap grows.
There's no continuous rotation or speed regulation: it's basically on or off, a push or a latch. Electrically, a motor draws a big inrush that decays as it speeds up.
A solenoid draws a pull-in current, then once the plunger seats, its inductance jumps and the current settles to V over R .
If you hold it on, it just burns I to the 2R as heat, so you often use peak-and-hold PWM to drop the holding current.
So I'd use a motor for continuous motion and a solenoid for short, fast, simple on/off actuation like valves, locks and latches."
